title: An encounter (Deus Caritas Est 1)
hookLine: being Christian begins with an encounter with a person
tomorrow: what could a girl sold as a slave find to hope in?

lines: NOT A RULE? NOT AN IDEA?
cards: Sign up for almost anything and the rules come first: terms, conditions, a box to tick before you're in. So here's an odd sentence from a pope.

Benedict the Sixteenth opens what he calls his first encyclical with a line from the first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him."
Then he says being Christian doesn't begin with an ethical choice. Or with a lofty idea. A pope, saying faith doesn't start with the rules?

teach.b: Here's how the puzzle comes apart. Benedict finishes the sentence. Being Christian, he says, is the encounter with an event, a person, who gives life a new horizon and a decisive direction.
So the order flips. Not a code first and a relationship later.

Someone is met, and the rest follows from the meeting. He points to John's Gospel, where God so loves the world that he gives his only Son. Then he does something quiet with the great command to love God and neighbor.
He doesn't drop it. Since God loved us first, he says, love is no longer only a command handed down from outside.
It becomes an answer: a response to a love that came looking first. The rules are still there; they've moved from the front door to the inside of a friendship.
One thing to tell a friend: the letter's name is just its first three Latin words, Deus caritas est, God is love. And in the next paragraph Benedict admits something honest.
The word love has been used and misused so much that it's worn thin. So he goes back to its source.

teach.h: GOD'S LOVE, THEN THE CHURCH'S CHARITY.
teach.b: The letter runs in two parts: God's love, then the Church's charity, love put to work for people in need.
Both stand on that first meeting.

how: Catholics who read Deus Caritas Est meet its opening as a starting point for prayer: faith begins with meeting Christ, and love of neighbor follows from it.

o: a sudden vision that proves God is real for good
meeting a person, Christ, as the place faith begins
a strict moral choice to follow the Church's rules

games.q: how the puzzle comes apart — tap the pairs.

s: for Benedict, the command to love is only a rule handed down from outside
since God loved first, he says, love becomes an answer to a love that came looking.
the letter is named for its first three Latin words
Deus caritas est: God is love.
the letter is all about feelings and never gets to people in need
its second part is the Church's charity: love put to work.

games.q: your cousin says he stopped going to Mass because it felt like a list of rules. what does Benedict's opening say comes first?
o: a clear set of moral rules, kept faithfully.
meeting a person, Christ; the rest follows from that.
a lofty idea about God that you agree with.
games.why: Benedict says being Christian isn't the result of an ethical choice or a lofty idea, but an encounter with a person. the commands become an answer to it.

practice: Close your eyes and let John's short line, God is love, sit there without explaining it. If you pray, turn toward him the way you'd turn toward someone who has just walked into the room, and say nothing for a while.
If not, stay with the memory of one person whose love found you before you'd earned it.

wordCard.voice: An encounter. Benedict's word for where Christian life begins: not a rule or an idea, but meeting a person.

orig.note: Latin for love, in the letter's title and first words: Deus caritas est, God is love.

carryVoice: The line to keep: an encounter, and the rules come after, as an answer. Day done.

sources.q: God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him.
